# Worksheet 3

## Welcome

This week covers two topics: 

1) Statistical power
2) Plotting data in R using ggplot2


> *Much of the materials builds on the running example introduced in Seminar 2: a 12-week weight-loss programme, compared with a control group, where the between-person SD of weight change is 5 kg and the smallest effect worth the cost of the programme is 2 kg. Trial A (n = 24 per group) found 4.37 kg, d = 0.87, t(46) = 3.03, p = .004. Trial B (n = 4,000 per group) found just 0.24 kg, d = 0.05, t(7998) = 2.17, p = .030: also significant, but far below the SESOI of 2 kg (Smallest Effect Size of Interest). You will learn today that the two trials differ sharply in power: Trial A had only 27% power to detect the SESOI (Smallest Effect Size of Interest), whereas Trial B's was effectively 100%. This session explains those numbers and gives you the tools to compute them for a study of your own.*

## Today's session

**Theory:** the four ingredients of statistical power; the `pwr` package and why "observed power" is circular; power
by simulation and why it generalises beyond what a formula can handle; why underpowered research drives the
replication crisis; three principles for communicating results through plots; the grammar of graphics.

**Practical:** two joint walkthroughs (power, then plotting), the same two topics as independent exercises, and an
optional Extra section (normal vs. t-distribution, R-tistry).

## Part 1: Joint walkthrough

We will work through this section together. Run each chunk as we go and make sure you understand the output before
moving on. As every week, start by loading the environment:

```{r}


library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(pwr)
```

### Section A: Power


#### 1.1 `qt()`: the quantile function of the t-distribution

You met `qt()` in Seminar 2 to find a critical value. Let's be precise about what it does, because the rest of this
section leans on it. `qt(p, df)` answers: *for a t-distribution with `df` degrees of freedom, what value has
probability `p` below it?* It is the exact mirror image of `pt()`, which you'll meet in a moment — `pt()` goes from
a value to a probability, `qt()` goes from a probability to a value.

```{r}
qt(0.975, df = 46)   # the value with 97.5% of the distribution below it (df = 46, Trial A)
qt(0.95, df = 46)    # the value with 95% below it — further left, since 95% < 97.5%
qt(0.5, df = 46)     # the median: by symmetry, exactly 0
```

`qt(0.975, df)` is the one you'll use constantly: it is the two-sided 5%-level critical value, because it leaves
2.5% in each tail (97.5% in the middle plus the 2.5% below it, 2.5% left over above).

```{r}
qt(0.975, df = 10)    # few degrees of freedom: heavier tails, a bigger critical value...
qt(0.975, df = 500)   # ...many degrees of freedom: close to the normal distribution's 1.96
qnorm(0.975)          # the normal distribution's version, for comparison
```

**Try it:** what is `qt(0.995, df = 46)` (the critical value for a 1%-level two-sided test), and is it bigger or
smaller than `qt(0.975, df = 46)`? Why does that make sense?

```{r}
# your code here
```

#### 1.2 Calculating power by hand

Now the real question: *if the programme's true effect really 2 kg, how likely is a study with
n = 24 per group to find it?* We build this up from exactly the quantities Seminar 2 already gave you — nothing new
except two functions.

```{r}
sd        <- 5      # between-person SD of weight change (both groups)
mean_diff <- 2       # the true effect we're asking about: the SESOI (Smallest Effect Size of Interest)
n         <- 24      # participants per group
```

**Step 1 — the standard error.** How much would the estimated difference vary from study to study, just
from sampling?

```{r}
se <- sd * sqrt(2 / n)
se
```

**Step 2 — degrees of freedom and the critical value.** From 1.1:

```{r}
df     <- 2 * n - 2 # since n is the same for both studies, otherwise n1 + n2
t_crit <- qt(0.975, df)
df
t_crit
```

**Step 3 — the threshold, in kg.** `t_crit` is in t-units. Multiplying by the SE turns it back into kilograms: any
estimated difference bigger than this would come out significant. Note that the threshold comes from H0 alone — it
doesn't care what the true effect is.

```{r}
thr <- t_crit * se
thr
```

So Trial A needs to observe a difference of at least about 2.91 kg to reach p < .05.

**Step 4 — where that threshold sits if the true effect is 2 kg.** If the programme really works, estimates from
studies like Trial A scatter around 2 kg (not 0), with the same SE. How far above 2 kg is the 2.91 kg threshold, in
SE units? That is just a t-score, computed under H1:

```{r}
t_h1 <- (thr - mean_diff) / se
t_h1
```

The threshold is only 0.63 SEs above the true effect.

**Step 5 — the areas, with `pt()`.** `pt(x, df)` gives the area to the *left* of `x`. To the left of the threshold, a
real 2 kg effect is missed (β); to the right, it is detected (power):

```{r}
beta  <- pt(t_h1, df)    # P(estimate below 2.91 kg | true effect = 2 kg): a miss
power <- 1 - beta        # P(estimate above 2.91 kg | true effect = 2 kg): a hit
beta
power
```

About 27%. The same picture in kilograms: the grey curve is H0 (centered on 0 kg), the blue curve is H1 (centered on
2 kg), the dashed line is the 2.91 kg threshold, and power is the shaded blue area to its right:

```{r}
kg <- seq(-6, 8, length.out = 400)
h0 <- dt(kg / se, df) / se                  # H0: estimates centred on 0 kg
h1 <- dt((kg - mean_diff) / se, df) / se    # H1: same shape, centred on 2 kg
plot(kg, h0, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "grey40",
     xlab = "Estimated difference (kg)", ylab = "density", main = "Power = blue area beyond the threshold")
lines(kg, h1, lwd = 2, col = "steelblue")
right <- kg >= thr
polygon(c(thr, kg[right], max(kg)), c(0, h1[right], 0), col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.3), border = NA)
abline(v = thr, lty = 2)
```

#### From kilograms to the noncentrality parameter (ncp)

Our 27% (`power` = 0.267) is very close to Seminar 2's 27.4%, but not identical. The difference comes from a shortcut
in Step 4: we simply slid the H0 t-shape over to 2 kg. Strictly, when H1 is true the test statistic follows a
slightly different, slightly skewed distribution called the **noncentral t-distribution**. It is described by one
extra number, the **noncentrality parameter (ncp)**: how far the centre of H1 sits from 0, in SE units — that is,
the true effect expressed as a t-value.

```{r}
ncp <- mean_diff / se
ncp
```

You have actually used it already: Step 4's `t_h1` is just `t_crit - ncp`.

```{r}
t_crit - ncp
t_h1
```

Here is what `ncp` looks like on the t scale: the grey curve is H0 (centred on 0), the blue curve is H1, and the
arrow is the shift between them, `ncp` = 1.39. The dashed lines are `±t_crit`.

```{r}
xs <- seq(-5, 8, length.out = 400)
plot(xs, dt(xs, df), type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "grey40", ylim = c(0, 0.47),
     xlab = "t", ylab = "density", main = "H1 is H0 shifted by ncp")
lines(xs, dt(xs, df, ncp = ncp), lwd = 2, col = "steelblue")
abline(v = c(0, ncp), lty = 3, col = c("grey40", "steelblue"))    # centres of H0 and H1
abline(v = c(-t_crit, t_crit), lty = 2)                            # the critical values
arrows(0, 0.43, ncp, 0.43, length = 0.08, code = 3)               # the shift = ncp
text(-0.15, 0.43, paste("ncp =", round(ncp, 2)), adj = 1)
```

R's `pt()` accepts an `ncp` argument, which gives the areas under the exact H1 curve. The test is two-sided, so
there are technically two ways to reject H0: far above `t_crit`, or far below `-t_crit`. The second is very unlikely
here, but we add it in for completeness:

```{r}
power_upper <- 1 - pt(t_crit, df, ncp = ncp)
power_lower <- pt(-t_crit, df, ncp = ncp)
power_by_hand <- power_upper + power_lower
power_upper
power_lower
power_by_hand
```

27.4% — exactly Seminar 2's number. In practice the kilogram method and the exact one agree to within a percentage
point or so; the exact one is what `pwr.t.test()` uses.

#### 1.3 `pwr.t.test()`: the one-line version

Only now, having done it by hand, bring in the package. The `pwr` package (Champely) does the calculation from 1.2
for you. Its function for t-tests, `pwr.t.test()`, links four quantities:

| Argument    | What it is                                              | Trial A          |
|-------------|---------------------------------------------------------|------------------|
| `n`         | participants **per group**                              | 24               |
| `d`         | effect size as Cohen's d: the true difference / SD      | 2 / 5 = 0.4      |
| `sig.level` | α, the false-positive rate you accept                   | 0.05             |
| `power`     | 1 − β, the chance of detecting the effect if it is real | what we want     |

These are the four ingredients from the slides, with one twist: the effect (2 kg) and the variability (SD 5 kg)
enter together as a single number, `d`. Only their ratio matters: a 2 kg effect with SD 5 kg is exactly as easy to
detect as a 4 kg effect with SD 10 kg.

The rule is: **give it any three, leave the fourth out, and it solves for the missing one.** Two further arguments
describe the design: `type` (`"two.sample"`, `"one.sample"` or `"paired"`) and `alternative` (`"two.sided"`
by default).

**Solving for power** (n known): how likely was Trial A to detect a 2 kg effect?

```{r}
pwr.t.test(n = 24, d = mean_diff / sd, sig.level = 0.05, type = "two.sample")
```

`power` should match `power_by_hand` from 1.2 to several decimal places — `pwr.t.test()` is running exactly the
noncentral-t calculation above, just taking Cohen's d (`mean_diff / sd`) instead of the two separately. Note the
reminder at the bottom of the output: `n` is the number in *each* group.

**Solving for n** (an *a priori* power analysis, done before collecting data): leave `n` out and supply `power`
instead, and it solves the equation the other way round — the n you'd need for 80% power:

```{r}
pwr.t.test(d = mean_diff / sd, sig.level = 0.05, power = 0.80, type = "two.sample")
```

The answer, 99.08, is not a whole number: always **round up**, so 100 per group (200 in total), roughly four times
Trial A's sample.

**Solving for d** (a *sensitivity analysis*, useful when n is fixed, e.g. by budget): leave `d` out. What is the
smallest effect Trial A had 80% power to detect?

```{r}
sens <- pwr.t.test(n = 24, sig.level = 0.05, power = 0.80, type = "two.sample")
sens$d          # in units of SD
sens$d * sd     # back in kilograms
```

Trial A could reliably detect only effects of about 4.1 kg or more, roughly twice the 2 kg that would make the
programme worthwhile. You can pull any single value out of the result with `$`, as here.

`pwr` has sibling functions that follow the same give-three-get-one rule for other tests, e.g. `pwr.r.test()`
(correlation), `pwr.anova.test()` (one-way ANOVA) and `pwr.chisq.test()` (chi-squared). For designs they don't
cover, use simulation (1.5).

#### 1.4 The observed-power fallacy

Trial A's own data gave d = 0.87, not the SESOI's (Smallest Effect Size of Interest) d = 0.40. What happens if you plug the *observed* effect back in?

```{r}
pwr.t.test(n = 24, d = 0.87, sig.level = 0.05, type = "two.sample")
```

84% power — reassuringly high. But this number is computed from the same data that produced the significant result
in the first place, so of course it looks good: a low p-value and a high "observed power" are two views of the same
fact, not two independent pieces of evidence. The honest version of this calculation is 1.2/1.3's: the power to
detect an effect you *specified in advance*, not the effect the data happened to hand you.

#### 1.5 Power by simulation

1.2 and 1.3 both work from a mathematical model of the t-distribution. Simulation instead *generates* many pretend
trials and simply counts how often the test comes out significant: no formula, no `ncp`, just `rnorm()` and
`t.test()`. We build it up one step at a time.

**Step 1 — write down what we assume is true.** A trial has two groups. For each we need a true mean and a true SD,
plus the number of participants per group. These are exactly the assumptions behind 1.2:

```{r}
n         <- 24   # participants per group
mean_ctrl <- 0    # true mean weight loss in the control group (kg)
mean_prog <- 2    # true mean weight loss in the programme group (kg): a real 2 kg effect
sd_ctrl   <- 5    # true SD in the control group (kg)
sd_prog   <- 5    # true SD in the programme group (kg)
```

**Step 2 — generate one pretend trial.** `rnorm(n, mean, sd)` draws `n` random values from a normal distribution with
that mean and SD. One call per group gives us one complete, made-up dataset:

```{r}
set.seed(18)     # makes the random numbers reproducible
control   <- rnorm(n, mean = mean_ctrl, sd = sd_ctrl)
programme <- rnorm(n, mean = mean_prog, sd = sd_prog)
mean(control)
mean(programme)
mean(programme) - mean(control)   # the estimated effect in this pretend trial
```

Let's look at it. The black line in each histogram is that group's sample mean:

```{r}
breaks <- seq(-25, 25, by = 2.5)   # same bins for both groups, so they are comparable
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))               # two plots side by side
hist(control, breaks = breaks, col = "grey80", main = "Control", xlab = "Weight loss (kg)")
abline(v = mean(control), lwd = 3)
hist(programme, breaks = breaks, col = "steelblue", main = "Programme", xlab = "Weight loss (kg)")
abline(v = mean(programme), lwd = 3)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))               # back to one plot per figure
```

The true difference is 2 kg, but the two sample means will not be exactly 2 kg apart: that is sampling error.

**Step 3 — analyse it, exactly as if it were real data.**

```{r}
test <- t.test(programme, control, var.equal = TRUE)
test$p.value
test$p.value < 0.05   # TRUE = significant: this pretend trial detected the effect
```

This pretend trial estimated the effect almost perfectly (about 2.1 kg), yet p ≈ .21: not significant. With
n = 24 per group, even a spot-on estimate of a real 2 kg effect falls short of the 2.91 kg threshold from 1.2.

**Step 4 — do it again.** Same assumptions, new random draw. The histograms change, the difference between the
means changes, and so does the p-value. Run this chunk several times and watch how often you get `TRUE`:

```{r}
control   <- rnorm(n, mean = mean_ctrl, sd = sd_ctrl)
programme <- rnorm(n, mean = mean_prog, sd = sd_prog)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(control, breaks = breaks, col = "grey80", main = "Control", xlab = "Weight loss (kg)")
abline(v = mean(control), lwd = 3)
hist(programme, breaks = breaks, col = "steelblue", main = "Programme", xlab = "Weight loss (kg)")
abline(v = mean(programme), lwd = 3)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

mean(programme) - mean(control)
t.test(programme, control, var.equal = TRUE)$p.value < 0.05
```

Even though the effect is real every single time, many runs come back non-significant. Each of those is a Type II
error (a miss).

**Step 5 — wrap one trial in a function.** Running chunks by hand gets tedious, so we package Steps 2 and 3 (minus the
plots) into a function that returns `TRUE` or `FALSE`:

```{r}
one_trial <- function(n, mean1, mean2, sd1, sd2) {
  group1 <- rnorm(n, mean1, sd1)   # control
  group2 <- rnorm(n, mean2, sd2)   # programme
  test   <- t.test(group2, group1, var.equal = TRUE)
  reject <- test$p.value < 0.05    # the same decision as comparing t_obs to t_crit in 1.2
  reject
}

one_trial(n = 24, mean1 = 0, mean2 = 2, sd1 = 5, sd2 = 5)   # one pretend trial: TRUE or FALSE
```

**Step 6 — repeat it many times and count.** `replicate()` runs the function 2,000 times. Power is simply the
long-run proportion of `TRUE`:

```{r}
set.seed(4)
decisions <- replicate(2000, one_trial(n = 24, mean1 = 0, mean2 = 2, sd1 = 5, sd2 = 5))
mean(decisions)   # the proportion of simulated trials that rejected H0
```

Compare this to `power_by_hand` (1.2) and `pwr.t.test()`'s answer (1.3) — all three should agree to within a
percentage point or two (simulation is noisy; more replicates would tighten it further).

Notice `one_trial()` takes the two groups' SDs *separately* (`sd1`, `sd2`), even though we gave it the same value
for both. The by-hand formula and `pwr.t.test()` both secretly assumed the two groups share one SD — try changing
`sd1 = 4, sd2 = 6` (keeping the same average spread) and rerunning: the simulation still works without changing a
single line, while the closed-form answer from 1.3 can no longer promise to be exact. This is the real payoff of
simulation: it keeps working once a design gets too complicated for a formula to exist.

### Section B: Plotting

#### 1.6 The three essentials

Every `ggplot()` needs three things: **data**, an **aesthetic mapping** (`aes()`, which variable goes where), and at
least one **geom** (the visual object). We'll use data from our running example: a simulated version of Trial A,
with 24 participants per group.

**Load the data.** The file is `seminar-03-power-and-plotting/seminar-03-worksheet_files/trial_a.csv`:

```{r}
trial_A_data <- read.csv(here::here("seminar-03-power-and-plotting", "seminar-03-worksheet_files", "trial_a.csv"))
```

**Explore it before plotting.** Always look at the data first: what the columns are, what type each one is, and
whether anything looks odd.

```{r}
glimpse(trial_A_data)   # one row per participant: columns and their types
head(trial_A_data)      # the first six rows
summary(trial_A_data)   # ranges, means, and any missing values (NA)
```

Each row is one participant: an `id`, their `group` (control or programme), `sex`, `age`, their weight at the start
(`baseline_kg`) and how much weight they lost over 12 weeks (`loss_kg`; a negative value means they gained weight).

How many participants are in each group, and in each group by sex?

```{r}
trial_A_data %>% count(group)
trial_A_data %>% count(group, sex)
```

And the numbers we actually care about, the mean and SD of weight loss in each group:

```{r}
trial_A_data %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), mean_loss = mean(loss_kg), sd_loss = sd(loss_kg))
```

**Now plot it.** A first question: did people who started heavier lose more weight? Data = `trial_A_data`, aesthetic
mapping = baseline weight on x and weight loss on y, geom = points:

```{r}
ggplot(trial_A_data, aes(x = baseline_kg, y = loss_kg)) +
  geom_point()
```



#### 1.7 Layer by layer: a boxplot that grows

Rather than jumping to a finished plot, build one up one layer at a time. Our main question: how much weight did
each group lose?

```{r}
# start
ggplot(trial_A_data, aes(x = group, y = loss_kg)) +
  geom_boxplot()
```

Notice that you can change the size of the plot in Quarto by modifying a header of the cell. Here, I added `fig.width=3, fig.height=4`\


```{r fig.width=3, fig.height=4}
# start
ggplot(trial_A_data, aes(x = group, y = loss_kg)) +
  geom_boxplot()
```

This is a nice plot but a bit boring. Next we will use the `fill` aesthetic to give it come colour. The fill aesthetic maps specific variable, in this case `group` to a property of the plot, in this case the color of the fill. Better, no? 

```{r fig.width=3, fig.height=4}
# add fill by group, and flip the coordinates so the groups run down the page
ggplot(trial_A_data, aes(x = group, y = loss_kg, fill = group)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) 
```

Notice how you can also flip the axes, in case you prefer.

```{r fig.width=4, fig.height=3}
# add fill by group, and flip the coordinates so the groups run down the page
ggplot(trial_A_data, aes(x = group, y = loss_kg, fill = group)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) + 
  coord_flip()
```

Each addition is one idea: `fill` maps a variable to colour (a **scale**), `coord_flip()` changes the **coordinate
system**. Nothing about the data changed between the two plots — only how it's shown!

#### 1.8 `geom_bar()` vs. `geom_col()`

```{r}
# geom_bar() counts rows for you
ggplot(trial_A_data, aes(x = sex)) +
  geom_bar()

```

Same picture, two different starting points: `geom_bar()` expects raw rows and counts them; `geom_col()` expects a
column of values already summarised (here, by `count()`).

Next step: adjust the y axis. `scale_y_continuous()` controls the y scale: `breaks` sets where the tick marks go,
`limits` sets the range shown, and `name` sets the axis title:

```{r  fig.width=3, fig.height=5}
ggplot(trial_A_data, aes(x = sex)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Number of participants",
                     breaks = seq(0, 30, by = 5),
                     limits = c(0, 30))
```

Only the axis changed; the bars are the same. Be careful with `limits`, though: any value outside the limits is
*removed* from the plot (!!!). Here every count fits between 0 and 30, so nothing is lost.

#### 1.9 Colour as a data-type decision

Colour is another aesthetic: just as `x` and `y` map columns to positions, `colour` maps a column to colours. Which
kind of palette you use depends on the **type** of that column, not on taste.

First, a **categorical** variable. `group` has two unordered levels, control and programme, so each level gets its own,
clearly different colour. `scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Set2")` picks a qualitative palette (distinct colours, none
"bigger" than another):

```{r}
ggplot(trial_A_data, aes(baseline_kg, loss_kg, colour = group)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Set2")
```

Now a **continuous** variable. `age` runs from the 20s to the 50s, so the colour should change gradually with it:
light-to-dark (or one hue to another) as age increases. `scale_colour_viridis_c()` is a sequential palette (the
`_c` stands for continuous), and it stays readable in greyscale and for colour-blind readers:

```{r}
ggplot(trial_A_data, aes(baseline_kg, loss_kg, colour = age)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_viridis_c()
```

Notice the legends: a set of separate keys for `group`, a continuous colour bar for `age`. ggplot2 chose these
because of the column types; the palette functions only control which colours are used.

#### 1.10 Faceting

Colour is one way to show the two groups in a single plot. Another is to give each group its own panel. 
`facet_wrap(~ group)` splits the data by `group` and draws the same plot once for each level, side by side and on
shared axes:

```{r}
ggplot(trial_A_data, aes(baseline_kg, loss_kg)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ group)
```

These are small multiples: easier to read than one crowded plot when there are many groups, and the shared axes keep
the panels directly comparable.

#### 1.11 Themes

Finally, the **theme** controls everything that isn't data: the background, gridlines, fonts and legend position.
ggplot2 has several complete themes; here we swap the default grey background for `theme_minimal()`:

```{r}
ggplot(trial_A_data, aes(baseline_kg, loss_kg, colour = group)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_minimal()
```

The points, colours and axes are exactly as before; only the look around them changed. This is the whole grammar,
end to end: data, aesthetics, geoms, scales, coordinates, facets, theme, each one a separate, swappable layer.

#### 1.12 Adjusting individual theme properties

A complete theme like `theme_minimal()` is a starting point. To change single properties, add `theme()` after it.
Inside `theme()`, each property is set with an *element* function that matches what kind of thing it is:

- `element_text()` for text (titles, axis labels): `size`, `face` (`"bold"`, `"italic"`), `colour`;
- `element_line()` for lines (gridlines, axis lines): `colour`, `linewidth`;
- `element_blank()` to remove something altogether.

Some properties take a plain value instead, e.g. `legend.position = "bottom"`.

Here we make the title bold, enlarge the axis titles, remove the minor gridlines, draw the axis lines, and move the
legend below the plot:

```{r}
ggplot(trial_A_data, aes(baseline_kg, loss_kg, colour = group)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Weight loss by starting weight",
       x = "Baseline weight (kg)", y = "Weight loss (kg)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
        axis.title       = element_text(size = 13),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        axis.line        = element_line(colour = "grey30"),
        legend.position  = "bottom")
```

Order matters: `theme()` must come *after* `theme_minimal()`, otherwise the complete theme overwrites your changes.

#### 1.13 Creating your own theme and reusing it

In a paper or thesis, every figure should look the same: same fonts, same gridlines, same legend position. Rather
than copying the same `theme()` lines into every plot, define the theme **once** and save it as an object. A theme is
just an R object, so it can be stored with `<-` like anything else:

```{r}
theme_paper <- theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +          # base_size sets all text sizes at once
  theme(plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold"),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        axis.line        = element_line(colour = "grey30"),
        legend.position  = "bottom")
```

The same idea works for colours: store the group colours once, so `control` and `programme` have the same colour in
every figure:

```{r}
group_colours <- c(control = "grey55", programme = "#1C68AB")
```

Now apply both to any plot by adding them with `+`. First a scatterplot:

```{r}
ggplot(trial_A_data, aes(baseline_kg, loss_kg, colour = group)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = group_colours) +
  labs(title = "Weight loss by starting weight",
       x = "Baseline weight (kg)", y = "Weight loss (kg)") +
  theme_paper
```

Then a completely different plot, a boxplot, with exactly the same look:

```{r}
ggplot(trial_A_data, aes(x = group, y = loss_kg, fill = group)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = group_colours) +
  labs(title = "Weight loss by group", x = NULL, y = "Weight loss (kg)") +
  theme_paper
```

To change the look of every figure later, edit `theme_paper` in one place and re-run. If you want a theme to apply to
*all* plots in a script without adding it each time, set it as the default once at the top:

```{r}
#| eval: false
theme_set(theme_paper)   # every ggplot() from now on uses theme_paper
```

## Extra (optional)

### Normal vs. t-distribution

Everything above used the t-distribution, the correct choice whenever the population SD is estimated from the
sample (as it almost always is). Here's what changes if you use the normal distribution instead.

**E1 — Critical values converge.**

```{r}
dfs <- c(5, 10, 30, 100)
data.frame(df = dfs, t_crit = qt(0.975, dfs), z_crit = qnorm(0.975))
```

As df grows, `qt()` gets closer to `qnorm()`'s fixed 1.96 — the t-distribution *is* the normal distribution, with
extra uncertainty built in for small samples.

**E2 — Using the normal for Trial A anyway.**

```{r}
se <- 1.44  # Trial A's SE, from Seminar 2
moe_t <- qt(0.975, 46) * se
moe_z <- qnorm(0.975) * se
c(t_based = moe_t, normal_based = moe_z)
```

The normal-based margin of error is a little too small — it understates the real uncertainty when n is this
modest, which is exactly why the t-distribution exists.

### R-tistry

"R-tistry" is generative art made entirely with R code — the same `ggplot2` grammar from Part 1, pointed at making
something to look at rather than something to read. Explore these first:

- [Rtistry Gallery — The Tidy Trekker](https://thetidytrekker.com/rtistry.html) — a gallery of finished pieces, for inspiration.
- [Thinking Outside the Grid](https://thetidytrekker.com/post/thinking-outside-the-grid/thinking-outside-the-grid.html) — a "bare bones" walkthrough of R-tistry concepts using plain `ggplot2`.
- [Generative art resources in R — Danielle Navarro](https://blog.djnavarro.net/posts/2021-10-19_rtistry-posts/) — a curated list of further tutorials and tools.
- [`aRtsy`](https://koenderks.github.io/aRtsy/) — a package that generates a finished piece from one line of code (e.g. `aRtsy::canvas_strokes()`), if you'd rather start from something and modify it.
